rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads the hereafter's gold, silk, couches, and green clothing allegorically as splendor, renewed life, and restful fulfilment after earthly self-denial.
rows.anchor: is obviously an allegory - in this case, an allegory of the splenddour, the ever-fresh life

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi distinguishes passive adornment, bestowed by God beyond the believers' deserts, from active clothing, earned through their deeds.
rows.anchor: Razi draws our attention to the difference in the construction of the two parts of this clause: the first part is in the passive form

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The garden parable connects with 18:7-8 and illustrates that earthly beauty is a means by which God tests people.
rows.anchor: This parable connects with verses 7-8 of this surah, and serves as an illustration of the statement that "all beauty on earth is a means by which God puts men to a test"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To be brought back or referred to one's Sustainer means being brought before Him for judgment.
rows.anchor: Lit., "brought back [or "referred"] to my Sustainer" - i.e., for judgment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to his discussions of the creation-from-dust statement at 3:59 and 23:12.
rows.anchor: See second half of note 47 on 3:59, and note 4 orr 23:12.

rows.speaker: Qiffal
rows.claim: Qiffal, as quoted by Razi, explains associating nothing with God as refusing to attribute wealth or poverty to any other creative power or cause.
rows.anchor: wealth or poverty with any power or creative cause other than Him" (Qiffal, as quoted by Razi)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means that the man had no host at all.
rows.anchor: Lit., "he had no host whatever".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final phrase literally means best as regards the consequence or outcome.
rows.anchor: Lit., "the best as regards the consequence".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words address people who denied resurrection during their lifetimes.
rows.anchor: to those who in their lifetime denied the truth of resurrection.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links this description to 6:94.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Adam prostration allegory stresses humans' inborn conceptual thought and their ability and duty to distinguish right from wrong.
rows.anchor: is meant, in the above context, to stress man's inborn faculty of conceptual thinking

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Attachment to worldly attractions lets Satan induce people to abandon moral considerations and suffer spiritual ruin.
rows.anchor: this attachment is the means by which Satan (or Iblis) induces man to forgo all moral considerations

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here, "invisible beings" denotes the angels.
rows.anchor: Denoting, in this instance, the angels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Satan's "offspring" is a metonym for all who follow him.
rows.anchor: Lit., "his offspring" - a metonym for all who follow him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means "for the evildoers"; Asad refers readers to notes on Satan's symbolic rebellion at 2:34 and 15:41.
rows.anchor: Lit., "for the evildoers". As regards Satan's symbolic "rebellion" against God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the beings invoked as masters are created rather than coexistent with God, they cannot be His equals or masters.
rows.anchor: since they are but created beings, and not co-existent with Me, how can you take them for your masters?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse alludes to real or imagined beings given divine qualities, whether consciously or through subconscious surrender to Satan's whispers.
rows.anchor: allusion to the beings, real or imaginary, to which men ascribe divine qualities

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since God is almighty, all-knowing, and self-sufficient, belief in partners in divinity or mediators between God and people leads them astray.
rows.anchor: the belief that any being or power could have a "helping" share in His divinity, or could "mediate" between Him and man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The supposed partners are beings people imagined to share in God's divinity; Asad links the phrase to 6:22.
rows.anchor: Lit., "those partners of Mine whom you supposed [to exist]": see note 15 on 6:22.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation makes the gulf a divide of unreality between sinners and the blasphemous figments of their imagination.
rows.anchor: wide gulf of unreality that separates those sinners from the blasphemous figments of their imagination

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari and Razi
rows.claim: Zamakhshari and Razi offer an alternative: the gulf separates sinners from saintly people they worshipped, who never claimed divine status; Asad considers this more probable.
rows.anchor: Zamakhshari and Razi in one of their alternative interpretations, with specific mention of Jesus and Mary

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad translates mathal as "lesson" here, following his explanation at 17:89.
rows.anchor: explaining my translation of mathal, in this context, as "lesson".

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari gives qubulan the senses "face to face" or "in the future"; Asad says both are contained in "the hereafter" or "the life to come".
rows.anchor: "face to face" or "in the future" (Zamakhshari)-: both these meanings of qubulan being comprised in the concept

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi explains forgetting what one's hands wrought as persisting in unrighteous conduct.
rows.anchor: I.e., persevering in his unrighteous behaviour (Razi).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally says "to guidance".
rows.anchor: Lit., "to guidance".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal wording says God would hasten punishment; the implication is that He gives sinners time to repent and mend their ways.
rows.anchor: the implication being that He invariably allows them time to repent and mend their ways.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maw'id can mean the end of sinners' earthly life or, as in 18:59, the point of no return beyond which they cannot sin with impunity; Asad compares 16:61 and 35:45.
rows.anchor: The "time-limit" (maw'id) signifies, in this context, the end of the sinners' life on earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording means that the communities had been doing wrong persistently and for a long time.
rows.anchor: Lit., "when [or "after"] they had been doing wrong" - i.e., persistently and for a long time.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders idh as "lo!" because it can mark a sudden turn in discourse without breaking continuity.
rows.anchor: The particle idh (which usually signifies "when", but is, I believe, properly rendered here as "lo!") often serves in the Qur'an to draw attention to a sudden turn in the discourse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The episode connects with 18:54 and allegorizes the inexhaustibility of knowledge, especially spiritual knowledge: no person, even a prophet, can answer every question in life.
rows.anchor: introduces an allegory meant to illustrate the fact that knowledge, and particularly spiritual knowledge, is inexhaustible

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad sets aside the innumerable legends that later grew around the Moses-and-knowledge parable as outside his concern.
rows.anchor: has become, in the course of time, the nucleus of innumerable legends with which we are not concerned here

rows.speaker: Ubayy ibn Ka'b
rows.claim: A tradition on Ubayy's authority says God rebuked Moses for claiming to be wisest and directed him to a wiser servant, with the disappearing fish as the sign of the destination.
rows.anchor: authority of Ubayy ibn Ka'b (recorded in several versions by Bukhari, Muslim and Tirmidhi), according to which Moses was rebuked

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads the fish in the tradition and Qur'anic account as an ancient religious symbol, possibly for divine knowledge or eternal life.
rows.anchor: The "fish" mentioned in the latter as well as in the above-mentioned hadith is an ancient religious symbol, possibly signifying divine knowledge or life eternal.

rows.speaker: early commentators
rows.claim: Early commentators tried to locate the two seas geographically, proposing sites from Bab al-Mandab to the Strait of Gibraltar.
rows.anchor: many of the early commentators endeavoured to "identify" in geographical terms

rows.speaker: Baydawi
rows.claim: Baydawi allegorically interprets the two seas as outward, observational and intellectual knowledge meeting intuitive, mystic insight; Asad calls their meeting Moses' real goal.
rows.anchor: Baydawi offers, in his commentary on verse 60, a purely allegorical explanation: the "two seas" represent the two sources or streams of knowledge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fata literally means "young man" and in early Arabic could mean one's servant regardless of age.
rows.anchor: Lit., "young man" (fata)- a term applied, in early Arabic usage, to one's servant (irrespective of his age).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tradition identifies the servant as Joshua, who later led the Israelites after Moses' death.
rows.anchor: According to tradition, it was Joshua, who was to become the leader of the Israelites after the death of Moses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Forgetting the symbolic fish may allude to people's frequent forgetting that God is the ultimate source of knowledge and life.
rows.anchor: is perhaps an allusion to man's frequently forgetting that God is the ultimate source of all knowledge and life.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idiom literally phrased as "Didst thou see?" conveys sudden recollection or surprise, like modern "Would you believe it?".
rows.anchor: Although formulated as a question, this idiomatic phrase often expresses - as does its modern equivalent, "Would you believe it?" - no more than a sudden remembrance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase literally means that Satan made the speaker forget it lest he remember it.
rows.anchor: Lit., "made me forget it lest I remember it".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fish's disappearance marked the place where Moses and his servant's quest was to end.
rows.anchor: the disappearance of the fish indicated the point at which their quest was to end

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the Ubayy tradition, the sage is called Al-Khadir or Al-Khidr, "the Green One"; Asad treats this as an epithet rather than a personal name.
rows.anchor: Ubayy ibn Ka'b (referred to in note 67) this mysterious sage is spoken of as Al-Khadir or Al-Khidr, meaning "the Green One"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Popular legend connects the epithet with ever-fresh, imperishable wisdom, supporting Asad's reading of the sage as an allegorical figure for the deepest mystic insight available to humans.
rows.anchor: his wisdom was ever-fresh ("green") and imperishable

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi reads the phrase as showing that even Moses did not fully comprehend the inner reality of things; Asad generalizes it to human unease before what is unfamiliar or incomprehensible.
rows.anchor: according to Razi, an allusion to the fact that even a prophet like Moses did not fully comprehend the inner reality of things

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage shows that appearance and reality can diverge and that people cannot grasp what has no counterpart in their intellectual experience, which explains Qur'anic metaphor and allegory for the unseen.
rows.anchor: appearance and reality do not always coincide; beyond that, it touches in a subtle manner upon the profound truth that man cannot really comprehend

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun "he" refers to the sage.
rows.anchor: Lit., "he".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording literally means that they asked the people of the village.
rows.anchor: Lit., "asked its people".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To cause a fault in the boat means to make it temporarily unserviceable.
rows.anchor: Lit., "to cause a fault in it" - i.e., to make it temporarily unserviceable.

rows.speaker: Taj al-'Arus
rows.claim: Taj al-'Arus notes that khashiya can mean having reason to fear and thus knowing that something bad will happen.
rows.anchor: khashiya sometimes denotes "he had reason to fear" and, consequently, "he knew", i.e., that something bad would happen (Taj al-'Arus

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad infers that the sage's "fear" meant positive knowledge, probably from mystic insight, as he later says he did not act on his own authority.
rows.anchor: the sage's expression of "fear" was synonymous with positive "knowledge" gained through outward evidence or through mystic insight

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The buried treasure was presumably an inheritance; had the wall fallen, avaricious villagers might have taken it, as their refusal of hospitality showed their character.
rows.anchor: left to them as an inheritance. Presumably that treasure would have been exposed to view if the wall had been allowed to tumble down
